titulo.texto: The Cloister and the Friars of the Convent

frase_gancho.texto: Orange trees, an enormous orchard and the friars who learned Nahuatl: the daily life of the Franciscan convent.

puente_narrativo.texto: Pass from the cloister to the rooms of the Museum of Sacred Art.

guion_corto.texto: A Dominican friar who arrived in Cuernavaca in fifteen eighty-five described the convent: it has a church, a cloister, dormitories and an orchard. A seventeenth-century chronicler added that the courtyard was adorned with orange trees and that the orchard was very large. The cloister is the central courtyard surrounded by galleries, and that is where the friars’ life took place. In the sixteenth century, figures such as Fray Toribio de Benavente, Motolinía, Agustín de la Coruña and Hernando de Leyva lived here. Francisco Cimbrón and Hernando de Leyva are buried in the convent. Today, the cloister’s galleries hold a large collection of Baroque art, mostly painting, spread across several rooms.

guion_largo.texto:
A cloister is a courtyard surrounded by covered galleries. In a convent, it was the center of daily life: the friars crossed it to go to the temple, the refectory and the dormitories. In the one in Cuernavaca, that courtyard changed uses, but it keeps its meaning.

Several people left descriptions of the convent. A Dominican friar, Father Ponce, who arrived in fifteen eighty-five, wrote that the building was finished and that it had a church, a cloister, dormitories and an orchard. In the seventeenth century, the chronicler Vetancurt described the courtyard decorated with orange trees and a very large orchard. He also wrote that the entrance hall, the portería, was more than fifty varas long.

In the sixteenth century, friars who later became very well known lived here. Fray Toribio de Benavente, whom the indigenous people called Motolinía, which means the poor one, was one of the first Franciscans to arrive in Mexico. He wrote a history of the peoples of New Spain. Agustín de la Coruña and Hernando de Leyva were also here. Two friars are buried in the convent: Francisco Cimbrón, of the province of the Conception, and Hernando de Leyva, of the province of Burgos.

The convent did not only keep people. Over time, the cloister became a space for a collection. In the galleries there is a large amount of Baroque art, mostly painting, spread across several rooms. A researcher, María Celia Fontana, has studied that collection. In it appear works attributed to Juan Correa, Juan de Miranda and Tomás de Sosa.

The cloister went through other changes. When the diocese was created in eighteen ninety-one, the old convent became a cathedral. In nineteen eleven, Bishop Francisco Plancarte y Navarrete founded a Museum of Sacred Art in Cuernavaca. In nineteen eighty-nine, the engineer Juan Dubernard cataloged the cathedral’s movable property. And in nineteen ninety-two, the Adopt a Work of Art program restored several key pieces. From the twenty-sixth to the thirtieth of October, two thousand two, the exhibition Artistic Treasures of the Cathedral of Cuernavaca was shown in the upper cloister.

To walk through it, think about what the day was like in a convent: prayer, meals, study and work. The covered galleries protected from sun and rain, and that is why the courtyard worked as everyone’s common room.

If you find works with their label, read it in full. The names of Correa, Miranda and Sosa appear in the studies of this collection, but not all attributions are certain. Pieces change place over time, and the open rooms can change too.

If the cloister is open when you visit, notice its silence. The friars walked it praying and studying. Whoever arrives today walks it differently, with head raised to see the ceilings and the arches, and at a slower pace. Now it is your turn to walk it looking.

texto: Walk along a gallery and try to imagine the friars crossing the courtyard
Look for the orange trees or the trees in the courtyard and think about the orchard Vetancurt described
Look at the paintings in the galleries and notice which ones have a Baroque religious theme

texto.pregunta: Myth: Motolinía was a mocking nickname.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was a Nahuatl name that the indigenous people gave him and that means the poor one, because of his humble life.
